1.pericope_label: Son of man, there were two women, the daughters of one mother: And they committed whoredoms in Egypt; they committed whoredoms in their youth
debates: Whether the elder sister is so called for age or size
What the two names signify
Why the sin is figured as whoredom
outliers: Gill, Ellicott and Wesley all take the word rendered elder for greater, Ellicott saying outright that it should be so translated and Gill that the ten tribes were more in number and greater in power and riches

The names are read as her own tabernacle and my tabernacle is in her, Ellicott because the northern kingdom set up its own worship instead of resorting to the Temple, Gill naming the calves at Dan and Bethel, and Wesley because the falling away from the house of David was a falling away from the tabernacle of God

Henry holds that representing the worst sins by whoredom intimates how exceedingly sinful uncleanness is in itself, since the worst of other sins are compared to it; Clarke reads the figure as aimed at exciting the utmost detestation of the crime
Keil and Delitzsch set out the structure of the whole chapter, the two sisters, the punishment of the elder, the worse harlotry of the younger, and a closing arraignment of both
themes: A God who speaks the same thing many a time, and all little enough
A kingdom so populous that it divided immediately upon the death of its king
Sisters so called because of their consanguinity
Children born to God by faith, love and obedience among the increase

5.pericope_label: And Aholah played the harlot when she was mine; and she doted on her lovers, on the Assyrians her neighbours
debates: How the clause about being his should be rendered
What her neighbours means
Whether famous is the right word
outliers: Gill offers three renderings, that she was his married wife, or under his cover and protection, or, with the Syriac, that she worshipped other gods besides him
Ellicott would render the word drawing near and holds the nearness spiritual rather than local, a sympathy in idolatry, since the same people are described later as coming from far
Ellicott holds notorious a better word than famous, the conquest of the city having by then made the northern tribes a byword among the nations
Ellicott takes the name of the northern power broadly enough to include Syria, as the counterpart to Egypt on the south
themes: A prophet compared to a Roman satirist as a rough reprover of abominable vices
A commentator who declines to take off the covering, since the details are not necessary to salvation
A colour put on soldiers because men finely arrayed are engaging to women fond of dress
A reality that breaks through the figure at the mention of idols

11.pericope_label: And when her sister Aholibah saw this, she was more corrupt in her inordinate love than she, and in her whoredoms more than her sister in her whoredoms
debates: Whether the younger sister exceeded the elder actually or only comparatively
What the girdles and head covering signify
Why the warriors are described so attractively
outliers: Ellicott holds the idolatries of the southern kingdom exceeded those of the northern not comparatively only but actually, citing the reign of Manasseh

Gill takes the girdles for a token of dignity and authority, the peculiar custom of the Babylonians as Kimchi reports from the Talmudists, and the head covering for turbans after the Persian manner; Wesley makes both military, soldiers belts standing for the whole habit of a soldier

Ellicott holds the warriors are drawn engagingly to carry out the figure and powerfully to explain the political attraction, the people being at once fascinated by their splendour and overawed by their power
Henry finds the perversity in the timing, that the southern kingdom was made worse rather than better by watching the destruction of the northern
themes: A kingdom that liked better the gods which would admit of partners
An altar copied from a foreign pattern and set up at home
Portraits once executed in brilliant colours on stone and on perishable brick
Exiles familiar with the very pictures the prophet describes

16.pericope_label: And as soon as she saw them with her eyes, she doted upon them, and sent messengers unto them into Chaldea
debates: What the word rendered paramours means
How widely the seeing should be taken
What the alienation of her mind was
outliers: Gill renders the word concubines and takes it of the nations allied to Egypt, reporting that the Septuagint and Arabic wrongly read the Chaldeans; Clarke gives harlots or concubines and notes that harlot anciently covered a prostitute of either sex; Ellicott insists the word is masculine and reads it of sins copied from the heathen
Ellicott takes the seeing widely enough to include knowledge obtained in any way, since many had seen the Babylonians in person and others knew of them by report

Ellicott says the original implies the disgust of satiety and traces a vacillation between Egypt and Babylon that at either turn failed of sole reliance upon God; Wesley says only that she grew weary of the Chaldeans
Gill reports that Jarchi referred the coming of the Babylonians to the ambassadors who were shown the treasures of the royal house
themes: Embassies implied by the history of which no special mention survives
A woman who casts off her former lovers and does not leave her lewdness
A king who perished in his zeal for the very power his kingdom later resented
Asses and horses introduced to show the intensity of the lust

22.pericope_label: The Babylonians, and all the Chaldeans, Pekod, and Shoa, and Koa, and all the Assyrians with them: all of them desirable young men
debates: Whether three names in the muster roll are places, peoples or titles
What the word rendered chariots means
What the cutting off of nose and ears signifies
outliers: Wesley treats the three names as geography and locates each; Ellicott holds them titles of officers with the Vulgate and most modern commentators, supporting this from their renderings elsewhere; Clarke surveys five explanations, including neighbouring peoples no geographer has found, and declines to settle the question

Ellicott holds the word occurs only here and is thought to mean a weapon, and would render the clause with weapons, chariots and wheels; Gill reports Jewish interpreters taking it for warlike instruments in general
Clarke and Ellicott agree the mutilation was an eastern punishment for adultery, Ellicott adding that it is named here with especial reference to destroying the attractiveness of the adulteress
Ellicott makes the correlation of punishment to sin the point of the passage, the alliance she sought for strength being the thing that overwhelmed her
themes: An indictment drawn in the form of an English criminal charge, with a plea of not guilty overruled
Lovers in one verse who are those she hates a few verses later
Spare wheels carried against a breakage on the march
A Latin epigram asking who counselled the cutting off of an adulterous nose

28.pericope_label: Because thou hast forgotten me, and cast me behind thy back, therefore bear thou also thy lewdness and thy whoredoms
debates: Who is said to do these things
How the cup should be measured
What the plucking of the breasts is
outliers: Gill notes that the Septuagint and the Vulgate render the clause in the third person, that they have done these things unto thee, where the Hebrew has God speaking in the first person

Wesley measures the cup by time, as containing what will last until the seventy years be expired; Ellicott measures it by shame, as drunk amid the derision of her neighbours; Gill by depth, as a cup that holds much

Clarke reads the plucking off of the breasts as a tearing, a frequent action in extreme sorrow along with weeping and beating the breast, and quotes a line of Ovid; Wesley reads it as the woman revenging herself upon herself
Wesley divides the bearing into the guilt which God will impute and the punishment which he will not pardon
themes: A threat repeated in different words for the greater certainty of it
Conquerors who hate as much as they were once loved
Dregs drunk not through love but by force
Shards broken to suck out whatever remains

36.pericope_label: Son of man, wilt thou judge Aholah and Aholibah? yea, declare unto them their abominations; That they have committed adultery, and blood is in their hands
debates: Whether the opening clause is a question or a command
Whether the adultery charged is literal as well as figurative
Why the two sisters are now judged together
outliers: Gill takes the opening as a question expecting no, forbidding the prophet to plead their cause or intercede; Ellicott would drop the interrogative and render it as the imperative judge thou; Henry gives both readings and prefers the second

Gill allows both senses of the adultery, either with the wives of their neighbours, which he says was a prevailing sin with this people, or the spiritual adultery which is idolatry; Henry takes it wholly of idolatry

Henry explains the joint judgment historically, that after the fall of the northern kingdom its remnant incorporated with the southern and many settled in the city, so that the two sisters had become one again
Ellicott notes that the figure is here partly dropped so that the reality may come out better
themes: A commission to judge read as a refusal of leave to intercede
Children passed through the fire not to be dedicated but to be devoured
Idolatry called a lusting after a carnal mind in the very worship of God
A sanctuary entered on the same day the children were offered

40.pericope_label: And furthermore, that ye have sent for men to come from far, unto whom a messenger was sent; and, lo, they came: for whom thou didst wash thyself, paintedst thy eyes, and deckedst thyself with ornaments
debates: What the voice of a multitude at ease means
What the stately bed is
Whether the following clause is a question
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott independently reject the received rendering, holding that the word never means the voice of a multitude but a loud tumult, so that the adjective must be the predicate and the sense is that the tumult was stilled; Ellicott adds that it was stilled by tribute. Gill and Wesley read a welcome instead, of ambassadors and their retinue greeted with shouts of joy, and Clarke an idolatrous festival with a riotous multitude
Gill allows a throne of state or a couch at a feast; Ellicott settles on the couch or divan; Clarke reads an altar raised to the idols, alluding to one made after a foreign pattern

Ellicott would not make the clause a question nor the next verse adversative, rendering it as a statement that her whoredom shall now be committed, since after all means of reclamation had failed God gave her up to her sins
Ellicott denies that the word rendered as a people in this verse is a proper name and takes it for drunkards, placed in the wilderness as the region they marched through rather than their home
themes: A modern eastern parallel offered for the washing, painting and adorning
Incense and oil that should have been the Lord alone turned to idols
Conquerors satisfied with tribute who then decked out their tributary with ornaments
A shifting between singular and plural explained by which sister was uppermost in the mind of the prophet

45.pericope_label: And the righteous men, they shall judge them after the manner of adulteresses, and after the manner of women that shed blood; because they are adulteresses, and blood is in their hands
debates: Who the righteous men are
Whether stoning is figure or fact
How the lewdness is made to cease
outliers: Four readings of the righteous men: Gill reports the prophets and righteous men in general before preferring the Babylonians, righteous only by comparison with a people who had revelation and knew better; Clarke names the same conquerors as appointed to execute judgment; Ellicott defines them as men to whom the judgment of righteousness is committed; Wesley takes them for men who keep the law of their God

Ellicott holds the figure and the reality are designedly mixed, since stoning was the legal punishment of adultery while the actual overthrow of the city was by the sword; Gill refers the stoning to the slings and engines of the besieging army
Gill, Clarke and Wesley read the ceasing as a historical outcome, that the people were never given to idolatry after the captivity; Ellicott explains it as ceasing by the removal of the sinners
Gill notes a variant in which the clause is not a promise but a command, the Targum representing the words as spoken to the prophet
themes: Conquerors called righteous only in comparison with those they punish
Stones from slings that killed some and brought houses down on others
All women read, in keeping with the allegory, as all nations
A judgment meant to stand for all time as a monument of righteous severity
